data.text: In the smartphone-ban debate, Mei argued the ban is a working-time intervention with real but modest test-score gains of about 0.05 to 0.1 standard deviations.
Mei argued enforcement costs fall on teachers and the kids who lose most already lack supervision elsewhere.
Mei closed that the ban is weaker than its advocates think and could support it only if the cap, enforcement, and override were defined.
Amara argued for phones off during instruction, taught use, and a spelled-out red-flag exception instead of a blanket ban.
In the compulsory-voting debate, Mei argued turnout gaps track registration rules and ease of voting, not mandates; fines fall on the poor, and coerced ballots are not consent.
Mei closed that design can fix fines but not the premise: pricing a right admits the invoice, not the claim, is the point, and compliant ballots are not consent.
Mei cited evidence that four-day week pilots are knowledge-work based and nearly silent on hospitals, transport and residential care, where service happens at fixed times.
Mei argued a nationwide four-day mandate redistributes labour rather than creating it: hire at recurring cost, or compress hours and hand the queue to stretched staff.
Mei measured extra staffed hours at 18–27% across nine shift-based organisations holding coverage constant; two of nine partially recovered costs through sickness and turnover.
Mei argued the 1931 Act phased over a decade with carve-outs, and the Working Time Code manages hours but does not pay for them.
Amara conceded the rota was paid for with longer shifts, said two of nine recovered part of the cost, and agreed sector trials should start with health and care.
